content_summary.series_and_form: Research article, Journal of the British Academy 14(3): a22, DOI 10.5871/jba/014.a22, published 21 Sept 2026, open access CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, 28 PDF pages (about 13,000 words incl. references). Footnote 1: 'based on my British Academy Keynes Lecture at Bristol University, 19 November 2025'; longer background paper = INET Oxford WP 2025-25 (18 Feb 2026, 54 pp; the working paper's abstract adds 'potential gains from a Green Land Value Tax' and 'politically feasible designs for less ambitious first steps'). Author declares no conflict, no funding, AI used only for literature searches. Not a working paper, book chapter or policy note.
content_summary.structure: 1 Introduction (pp.1-6; Muellbauer's own research history from the 1987 Poll Tax critique); 2 Land and housing institutions and the Thatcher reforms of the 1980s (pp.6-9: financial deregulation; regulation and taxation of land and housing); 3 Impact on growth, fiscal capacity and financial stability (pp.9-12); 4 The UK's housing affordability problem (pp.12-17); 5 A holistic policy package (pp.17-22: planning reform; land-value capture; expanding social housing; benefits of tax reform and a green land-value tax); Conclusions (pp.21-22); notes and references.
headline_claims_with_named_sources: Land share of housing value: 'for an average British house, around 70 per cent of the value is in the land rather than the structure' (p.9), from ONS household balance-sheet data; Fig. 2 (OECD national accounts) shows the UK highest in the G7 at over 70%. Fn 14 concedes the share depends on national-accounts depreciation conventions for buildings but argues international comparison is little affected. (Matches the wiki's existing 70% claim from the 2023 paper.)

Real house prices: UK rose most among the G7 since 1982, about 300% (Fig. 1, OECD real house price index relative to 1982Q1; p.3-4). Muellbauer infers 'even greater rises in real land prices' because building costs are relatively stable (p.4, p.10); this is inference, not a measured land-price series.

Demand-side decomposition (Fig. 5, p.15): using an income-to-housing-stock elasticity of 1.8 from Duca, Muellbauer & Murphy (2021, J Econ Literature), 63% of the rise in UK real house prices 1980-2025 is explained by real household income relative to the housing stock (ONS series, net capital stock MLO9). A 1% increase in the housing stock, about a year's residential investment, lowers real prices only 1.8% (p.16). Contested: he rejects Mulheirn (2019) 'no supply problem' (citing Cheshire's critique) and says Miles & Monro (2021) overstate the interest-rate channel (pp.15-16).

Council housing: 2.8 million council homes sold by 2006, about half the stock (p.13); social-rented share of households fell from 29% (1979) to 16% (2022-3) (p.17); owner-occupation 55% (1979) to 72% peak (2001) then falling, 25-34s peaking at 50% in 1989 (Fig. 6, Corlett & Odamtten 2021, Resolution Foundation).

Productivity and crowding-out evidence he relays (pp.10-12): Müller & Verner (116 countries, 1940-2016, credit to non-tradable sectors in real-estate booms); Doerr 2020 (BIS WP 904); Chakraborty, Goldstein & MacKinlay 2018 (RFS); Hau & Ouyang 2024 (China); Grjebine, Héricourt & Tripier 2023 (33 sectors, 14 countries, UK/Ireland/France/Spain TFP losses); NERA 2024 for the Mayor of London (142 local authorities, 2002-21: a 1% fall in house-price-to-income ratio raises local productivity 0.14%) and Homes England 2025 (0.31% for London and the greater South East); Hirano & Stiglitz (2025) OLG model of land speculation curtailing long-run growth. He criticises Black, de Meza & Jeffreys (1996) as reaching a wrong policy conclusion (p.12). Fn 15 cites Maclennan et al. 2021 that causal attribution across channels is unreliable.

Fiscal and stability: tax cost of housing-related benefits GBP 26.8bn in 2021-2 (Chartered Institute of Housing, UK Housing Review 2024; p.13); UK mortgage market dominated by adjustable/short-fix loans, so vulnerable to rate jumps 2021-5 (p.12).

Development Land Tax: abolished March 1985 (introduced 1976); Muellbauer, citing Gibson (2025: 98), says the abolition 'probably contributed' to the 1985-9 land and house price boom (p.6). Pre-announced abolition of Domestic Rates 'probably gave a significant fillip' to the boom from 1986 (p.8). Agricultural Property Relief (Inheritance Tax Act 1984) is called an avoidance route that drives up land prices (p.8). These tie directly to the DLT repeal already in concepts/betterment-levy.md (abolished 19 March 1985).

policy_package.planning_reform: Relies on Cheshire (2018, 2024) and Cheshire & Carozzi (2019); Watling & Breach (2023) flexible zoning code; Auckland 2016 upzoning (Greenaway-McGrevy & Phillips 2023: more building, slower rent rises); cooperatives and community land trusts (Forest City could become Europe's largest CLT); Falk (2025) devolution to city/region (p.18).
policy_package.land_value_capture_instruments_named: Defined as capturing 'for the taxpayer most of the increase in land value' from planning permission and infrastructure (p.18). Instruments and measures named: further reform of the Land Compensation Act 1961 beyond the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 to cut 'hope value' in compulsory-purchase compensation and widen who may use CPO; public land and property counted in the public-sector net-worth fiscal rule (2024 shift from gross debt); tougher Section 106 affordability conditions and higher build-out rates; New Towns / development corporations (1946, 1965 Acts; Docklands, Merseyside); Community Infrastructure Levy (2008 Act, from 2010) acknowledged; fn 28 summarises the Commons HCLG Committee 2025 report (HC 672) recommending S106 and CIL reform, land-value transparency and CPO powers for New Town corporations. He says LVC is 'stalled' (p.21).
policy_package.social_housing: Cites Shelter (2025), National Audit Office (2022) long-run return of GBP 2.70 per GBP 1 invested in affordable homes (p.19); government's June 2025 GBP 39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme over ten years from 2026-7 (fn 29). No Muellbauer-own target number for homes per year; building targets are called 'unrealistic' (p.21). Argues social housing investment must be paired with LVC and planning reform.
policy_package.property_tax_reform: Council Tax on 1991 values with banded cliff edges, regressive locally and regionally (Adam et al. 2020 IFS; Corlett & Gardiner 2018; Dixon et al. 2021 Fairer Share); Stamp Duty progressive but calcifies the market; Cook (2025) Fig. 7 shows the two roughly offset (p.19). Calls for simultaneous reform: immediate halving-type Stamp Duty cut plus an announced proportional property tax (cuts cannot be pre-announced) (p.19). Deferral: equity-style right to defer for every retired household with an interest registered at the Land Registry; 0.5% for payers vs 0.6% for deferrers yields about 6% of sale value after ten years (p.21). Footnote 30 calls the 2025 Budget High-Value Council Tax Surcharge 'poorly designed' but notes it opened a window for revaluation (Muellbauer 2026c, FT).
policy_package.match_with_wp_2026_24: Overlaps but does not repeat: shares the immediate Stamp Duty cut, the 0.5%/0.6% deferral numbers and the HVCTS criticism with WP 2026-24 (the wiki's existing page); does NOT carry WP 2026-24's PHVCTS rates (0.5%/1% above GBP 1.5m), taper formula or GBP 2.2bn revenue estimate. Adds what WP 2026-24 omits: the land-share, macro/credit and productivity argument, the LVC section, the social-housing case, and the LVT / Green LVT discussion.

content_summary.land_value_tax_specifically: Yes, a page-length passage (pp.19-21). Defines LVT as a levy on land value only; cites Churchill's 1909 speech; relays the OECD (2022, Housing Taxation in OECD Countries) point that because land supply is highly inelastic, taxes on unimproved land are economically efficient unlike taxes on improvements (p.20); says shifting Business Rates to LVT 'would be particularly beneficial for economic efficiency and growth' citing Muellbauer (2005, IPPR 'Time for Land Value Tax?') and the Mirrlees Review (2011). Green Land-Value Tax (his 2023 OECD chapter / INET WP 2023-12 'Why we need a green land value tax'): a split-rate property tax, charge on land plus charge on building minus a discount tied to carbon emissions (EPC); needs a revaluation separating land from building values, as Germany recently did; acknowledges separation difficulty in the UK given planning-induced land value differences but says automated valuation, AI and granular data have improved accuracy (p.20). Feasible short-term goal: proportional property tax with green discounts PLUS a land tax on high-value unbuilt and agricultural land (example threshold above GBP 40,000 per hectare), to improve build-out and land release for New Towns; requires registration of all land options at the Land Registry (Lyons Review 2014; Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023) (p.21). The working paper (WP 2025-25 s.6.4, pp.34-37) adds the reasoning: land prices more volatile than building costs so stability improves; land more unequally distributed than property; two objections to a PURE household LVT (buildings drive emissions; Mirrlees: housing is a durable consumption good so property tax should partly fall on buildings); five-year phased transition. The JBA article is the short form of that argument.

quotes_50_words_or_less.text: We probably have the most regressive annual property tax in the world.
for an ‘average’ British house, around 70 per cent of the value is in the land rather than the structure.

Credit-fuelled real-estate booms crowd out more productive investment, and the benefits of growth then disproportionately accrue to the owners of land through higher land prices and to the credit-providing financial sector.
Land-value capture (LVC) seeks to secure for the taxpayer most of the increase in land value that arises from two primary drivers: changes in planning permission and infrastructure investment.
A feasible short-term goal would be the combination of a proportional property tax on residential property with green discounts, and a land tax on high-valued unbuilt land and agricultural land.
Taxing high-value idle land and farmland could accelerate build-out, lower land prices, diminish landowners’ bargaining power, and thus support sustainable housing.

content_summary.page_locator_note: Locators are PDF page numbers of the JBA PDF (28 pp); the HTML version has section headings but no page numbers. Section numbers 2-5 given above.

(c) research/ryan-collins-rethinking-land-housing.md and concepts/financialization-of-land.md (both read in full) carry the land-credit feedback loop from the 2017 book only (financialization page: lending shares 35%->10%, 25%->50%); neither cites Muellbauer beyond the book's foreword (Ryan-Collins page) nor the Müller-Verner / Doerr / Grjebine crowding-out literature. (d) places/united-kingdom.md (read) cites Ryan-Collins for land-price multiples and links the WP 2026-24 page; no Thatcher-era institutional narrative, no DLT-1985 link to house prices. (e) concepts/betterment-levy.md already has the 1976 DLT and its abolition on 19 March 1985 (Gibson 2025 as source) and S106/CIL, so the article adds only Muellbauer's causal claim about the abolition. (f) concepts/land-value-capture.md has England only via the CaCHE Shepherd & White item and McAllister; no Muellbauer. (g) The wiki does not carry INET WP 2025-25 (the background paper) or the 2023 INET WP 2023-12 as pages; the 2023 paper appears only as a source in people/john-muellbauer.md. (h) Related, already on the wiki: research/hirano-stiglitz-credit-land-speculation-growth.md (the Hirano & Stiglitz model the article relays), research/letwin-build-out-review.md (build-out rates), events/right-to-buy.md, concepts/hope-value.md (stub), research/mirrlees-review.md. No existing page duplicates the article.
uncertainties: Peer-review process is not stated on the JBA page; the 'Article timeline' (Received Oct 2022, Accepted May 2023, Published July 2023) is stale template data from another item. Cite the 21 Sept 2026 publication date only.

Most figures are relays of other authors' work (NERA, Homes England, NAO, CIH, Resolution Foundation) read only as cited in the article; Tier 1 usable only 'as reported by Muellbauer' unless the underlying source is fetched. The NERA 0.14% / Homes England 0.31% are elasticities of productivity to the price-to-income ratio.

The Fig. 5 decomposition (63%) rests on an assumed elasticity of 1.8 and an income-to-stock specification; the author says only half of 1995-2018 growth is explained by supply failure, so the 63% is for 1980-2025 and should not be paraphrased as 'supply explains 63%'.

'Land prices rose more than house prices' is inferred from stable building costs plus a house-price series, not from an ONS land-price series; the 70% figure depends on national-accounts depreciation assumptions (fn 14).
He is also the author of the cited background paper and of several works he relies on (Muellbauer 2018, 2023, 2024, Duca-Muellbauer-Murphy 2021): self-citation weight.
The article is policy advocacy as well as synthesis (the Keynes Lecture format); the planning, social-housing and LVC recommendations are not tested.

Wiki editors should treat 'the Thatcher-era reforms caused it' as the author's interpretive thesis; the article itself cautions that productivity causality cannot be allocated across channels (fn 15).
The Thatcher-era political framing (e.g. 'largely for the worse', 'populist right' paragraphs) is the author's; keep the page's lead to the empirical claims and package, attribute framing.

verdict: ENRICH concepts/betterment-levy.md (International Context: one sentence on the Philippine special levy anchored on RA 7160 ss.240-241, with the statutory cost cap, and the peer-reviewed capacity finding) and concepts/land-value-capture.md (Instruments or Recent Case Studies: a short Philippines bullet carrying the Muntinlupa case as a journalist-author's argument, origin only). Do NOT create places/philippines.md: the Tier 1 material is one statute, one abstract-only peer-reviewed study (Samantela & Maquiling 2024) and the existing Baybay mass-appraisal page, which is about valuation method and not about capture; the Muntinlupa case is Tier 2 and unreviewed. A hub would rest on one statute and two thin pages. Revisit places/philippines.md if the Samantela & Maquiling full text, SB 1824's status or a BLGF/Muntinlupa primary is obtained. Not REJECT: the statute is a genuine, verifiable Tier 1 primary and fills a gap (no Philippine capture instrument anywhere on the wiki), and the case is a usable illustration of why a cost-capped special levy is weaker than uplift capture. Suggested wording for editors (impersonal, no process narration): (1) betterment-levy.md: 'The Philippines' Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7160, s. 240) lets a province, city or municipality impose a special levy on land specially benefited by public works it has funded, capped at 60 per cent of the actual cost of the works, including land acquisition, and payable in annual instalments of not fewer than five nor more than ten years (s. 241). Because the ceiling is set by project cost and not by the land-value uplift, the instrument recovers costs rather than capturing the increment. A 2024 qualitative study of Metro Manila local governments reports that the levy is rarely used, citing institutional, financial and technical capacity constraints.' (2) land-value-capture.md bullet: 'Muntinlupa, Philippines (2026). A journalist-author, Juan V. Sarmiento Jr., reports an unreviewed difference-in-differences estimate that a roughly PHP 39 million city-funded access road (CARES), opened in 2013, was followed by about PHP 476 million of additional land value in Pleasant Village relative to a comparison subdivision, none of which the city has recovered although s. 240 of RA 7160 would allow a special levy; a council member quoted in the report says the road was built to ease traffic and that new taxes are politically sensitive.' Pair (2) with the caveats in uncertainties. Statutory cap arithmetic (analysis, not in the article): if PHP 39 million is the full project cost, the s. 240 ceiling would be about PHP 23.4 million, roughly 5% of the PHP 476 million estimate; this is the editor's calculation and should be flagged as such if used.
claim_grade: C for the Muntinlupa uplift figures (empirical; a small-N descriptive difference-in-differences by a Tier 2 journalist-author on deeds-of-sale prices that the author says may be under-declared; not peer-reviewed; tables not seen; underlying data not published). B for the statutory claims once checked against RA 7160 (A-claim for the text of ss.155, 240, 241 from LawPhil: Tier 1 statute); the article's reading of the statute is partly wrong (see uncertainties). Source tier under 4c: Sarmiento = Tier 2 (journalist: 30 years as Inquirer reporter and editor; UP BS Statistics and master's in property valuation and management; wrote this as a news-feature on his own paper) — origin or proponent of the case only, never support. Coverstory.ph is an independent Philippine online news outlet (Tier 2/3 as a venue). The KKK seminar is NOT a peer-reviewed academic series.

content_summary.seminar_and_authorship: Single author: Juan V. Sarmiento Jr. (the article is his summary of his own paper; no co-authors named). Per the article's closing note, he presented it on 5 Oct 2026 at the 51st Sustainable Shared Growth (KKK51) Seminar, 'jointly organized by UP Open University's Faculty of Management and Development Studies and SGRA PH Sekiguchi Global Research Association of Atsumi Zaidan', which 'piggybacked on' the three-day 4th International Forum on Sustainability Science at Pampanga State Agricultural University. Series check (KKK50 report, July 2026; UPOU/FMDS pages via web search): the KKK (the three goals are efficiency, equity and environment, per search summaries of the series) seminars are convened by the Sekiguchi Global Research Association (SGRA) of the Atsumi International Foundation (Tokyo) in collaboration with the Faculty of Management and Development Studies, University of the Philippines Open University; the 50th (July 2026) had student, practitioner and faculty presentations on local-to-local cooperation, i.e. a workshop-and-report series, not a refereed journal or conference. A written paper may exist in the KKK51 report (not yet posted at the series' usual URL as of 12 Oct 2026). Seminar-paper availability online: not found.
content_summary.cares_road_facts: City Alternative Route Entry and Exit System (CARES): built by the Muntinlupa city government 'at an estimated cost of PHP 39 million'; 'it was assumed that the city had paid for the right of way' (the article does not confirm); opened to traffic in 2013, linking Pleasant Village and eight other subdivisions to the 244-hectare Filinvest City central business district in Barangay Alabang (later 11 subdivisions benefiting, two integrated only in 2018). Road length: not stated. Reported effects: travel time to the CBD under a minute; more than 6,000 motor vehicles redirected to the route (source not named); private sticker fees are charged by Pleasant, other subdivisions and Filinvest Alabang Inc., the city 'gets nothing'; government vehicles pass free. Official record: Muntinlupa Resolution No. 2023-352 (Sangguniang Panlungsod; sponsor Councilor Raul R. Corro) recites that Ordinance 02-045 'established the City Alternate Route and Entry System also known as C.A.R.E.S.' as an interconnection of listed subdivisions ending at Filinvest Corporate City, and authorises a tripartite memorandum of agreement with homeowners' associations to open a further passageway as part of 'the existing C.A.R.E.S. system'. So the network is built by agreement over subdivision roads, not purely as a city-owned road; the ordinance number suggests a 2002 origin (inferred from the number, not stated), with the 2013 opening as the Pleasant link per the article.
land_price_figures_with_named_sources: Zonal values in Pleasant: PHP 2,400 per sq m in 2007-2013 to PHP 12,000 per sq m in 2014 (BIR zonal values, as reported; a subdivision without CARES access rose by less; no figure given).

Descriptive DiD (author's estimate, Pleasant treated vs Lakeview comparison, average land-sale prices per sq m in 2010 and 2016, from Assessor's Office deeds of absolute sale, with random and purposive samples; outliers, donations, extrajudicial settlements, dacion en pago and multi-lot sales excluded): PHP 5,645 per sq m; about PHP 1.7 million extra value for an average 300 sq m lot; PHP 476 million aggregate for the subdivision (implies about 280 lots at that average, not stated). Arithmetic check: 5,645 x 300 = PHP 1.69m; PHP 39m / PHP 476m = 8.2%, matching the article's 'only 8.2% of private land-value gains'.

Asking or market prices of vacant lots per sq m in Pleasant: 2014 PHP 5,000; 2016 PHP 13,000; 2017 PHP 17,000; 2019 PHP 20,000; 2021 PHP 25,000-31,000; 2026 a Mandarin Avenue lot offered at PHP 70,000 (agents and residents, not declared deed prices). The author says deed prices are lower, probably because sellers under-declare to reduce capital gains and documentary stamp tax.

Causal caveat: the DiD compares one treated and one comparison subdivision over two years with no control for other changes (Filinvest City growth, PLDT 5-hectare site bought 2025, the 2018 integration of two further subdivisions). The author does not report confidence intervals or placebo tests.

statutory_provisions_checked_against_law.section_240_special_levy: Verbatim (LawPhil text): 'A province, city or municipality may impose a special levy on the lands comprised within its territorial jurisdiction specially benefited by public works projects or improvements funded by the local government unit concerned' with a proviso that the levy 'shall not exceed sixty percent (60%) of the actual cost of such projects and improvements, including the costs of acquiring land and such other real property in connection therewith', and does not apply to lands exempt from basic real property tax or to lands donated for the project. (first quote about 40 words, second about 30 words; both under 50.)
statutory_provisions_checked_against_law.section_241_instalments_and_rates: The 5-10 year collection period the article attributes to s.240 is in s.241: the ordinance must state the estimated cost, the metes and bounds, and 'the number of annual installments for the payment of the special levy which in no case shall be less than five (5) nor more than ten (10) years'; the sanggunian 'may fix different rates for different parts or sections thereof, depending on whether such land is more or less benefited' (not obliged to use a uniform percentage). s.242 requires a public hearing and written notice to owners; s.243 apportions the levy 'according to the assessed valuation of the lands affected'; s.244 gives owners the real-property-tax remedies; s.245 accrual from the first day of the quarter after the ordinance takes effect.
statutory_provisions_checked_against_law.section_155_not_general_user_fees: The article calls s.155 'user fees'. The text is headed 'Toll Fees or Charges': the sanggunian 'may prescribe the terms and conditions and fix the rates for the imposition of toll fees or charges for the use of any public road, pier, or wharf, waterway, bridge, ferry or telecommunication system funded and constructed by the local government unit concerned', with exemptions for AFP and PNP personnel on mission, postal workers delivering mail, and disabled citizens aged 65+; the sanggunian may discontinue collection when public safety and welfare so requires. This is a road-toll power, relevant to a CARES access fee only if the roads are LGU-funded and LGU-constructed.
statutory_provisions_checked_against_law.statutory_design_point: The s.240 ceiling is set by project cost (60% of actual cost, land acquisition included), not by the land-value gain, and the levy is apportioned by assessed value, so it is a cost-recovery special assessment, not an uplift capture: on the article's own figures a full-cost levy could never reach more than a small fraction of the estimated windfall. The wiki's treatment of Colombia's valorizacion (benefit-factor apportionment, cost cap) is the closest comparator.
statutory_provisions_checked_against_law.possible_later_change: RA 12001 (Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act, signed 13 June 2024; LawPhil https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2024/ra_12001_2024.html) moves to a single market-value basis and a BLGF-led schedule of market values; whether it alters the assessed-value base in s.243 for special levies was not checked.

content_summary.four_step_roadmap: As recommended by the author (a two-pronged benefit-based approach: asset-based taxation for land-value gains, consumption-based pricing for road wear): (1) adopt a phased special levy after strengthening the Assessor's Office capacity for a comprehensive capitalization and benefit assessment of CARES-affected properties; differentiated rates by degree and timing of benefit across the 11 subdivisions, with the two integrated only in 2018 not liable for earlier periods; (2) introduce consumption-based user charges, such as electronic road pricing or an access fee differentiated by use; (3) establish a dedicated infrastructure and maintenance fund earmarked from levy and charges; (4) institutionalize land-value effects in evaluation and financing of future transport projects.
content_summary.political_position: Councilor Raul Corro, author of the CARES ordinance, is quoted that CARES 'is viewed primarily as a traffic-management solution' and that the council is careful about new taxes because it is 'a big political issue'. The article calls this a 'policy blind spot'. No Council ordinance or budget document on a levy was found.
tier_1_primaries_identified: RA 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991), LawPhil full text: ss.155, 240-245 (and ss.212-218 on the schedule of market values and assessment, s.232 basic real property tax).
Muntinlupa Sangguniang Panlungsod Resolution No. 2023-352 (recites Ordinance 02-045 establishing CARES).

Samantela, S.S. & Maquiling, K.S.M., 'Examining Institutional Challenges of Land Value Capture: The Case of Implementing Land-based Taxes in the Philippines', DOI 10.22004/ag.econ.340794 (AgEcon Search record 340794; the PDF is named JHES_2_1_7, i.e. the Journal of Human Ecology and Sustainability, UP Los Baños; year about 2024 per search summaries). Per the AGRIS abstract: the special levy exists in the Code but is rarely used; a literature review plus semi-structured interviews and a self-assessment scoring exercise with staff of Metro Manila cities find institutional, financial and technical capacity barriers and weak understanding of LVC in local public finance; recommends capacity building and better land-valuation arrangements. Full text not read.

Senate Bill No. 1824 (19th Congress), 'Land Value Capture Act', Sen. Imee Marcos, filed 31 January 2023, referred 6 Feb 2023 to Local Government, Justice and Human Rights, and Finance (per Senate legislative-record summary via search); would have the Bureau of Local Government Finance set uniform valuation standards for special levies. Bill text not read; later status unknown; a filed bill is evidence of the gap, not of law.

existing_wiki_coverage: Corpus digest (1027 pages), direct reads and grep. No page covers the Philippines' fiscal system or any Philippine capture instrument: the only Philippine page is research/bencure-ilvm-baybay-philippines.md (read in full), a 2019 AHP mass-appraisal paper for Baybay City (valuation method, 'developing-country mass-appraisal' evidence), with no mention of special levies or RA 7160. concepts/land-value-capture.md (read in full) lists 'betterment levies / special assessments' generically and has no Philippine, Muntinlupa or road-uplift case; its nearest road/transit items are Grand Paris Express, Transbay TIF, São Paulo OODC/CEPAC, Warsaw metro (hedonic 6.7-7.1%) and London (TfL/GLA: Jubilee Line Extension 52%, DLR 23%, North London Line 6% uplifts). concepts/betterment-levy.md (read in full) is UK-centred with an International Context paragraph naming Colombia's contribucion de valorizacion, Germany's Wertzuwachssteuer, Taiwan's LVIT and Victoria's Windfall Gains Tax, with no Asian special-assessment statute. concepts/valorization-tax.md is the wiki's special-assessment comparator (cost-capped, benefit-factor apportionment). research/india-mohua-value-capture-framework.md and concepts/land-pooling.md cover South Asian instruments. problems/public-investment-capitalizes-into-land.md holds the capitalization evidence the Muntinlupa case would illustrate. people/julio-senador-gomez.md mentions the Philippines only incidentally. Nothing on KKK seminars, Sarmiento or Coverstory.
uncertainties: Tier: Sarmiento is a journalist with a relevant master's (UP property valuation and management) and a working-economist-journalist track record, but the work is an unreviewed seminar paper presented to a non-peer-reviewed seminar series (KKK convened by SGRA/Atsumi Foundation with UPOU FMDS); under 4c cite as origin or proponent only, 'a journalist-author's estimate'.

The article misattributes provisions: the 5-10 year collection period is s.241, not s.240; s.155 is a toll-fee power over LGU-funded and LGU-constructed roads, not general 'user fees'. The statutory quotes should come from LawPhil, not from the article. Also unmentioned by the article: s.240 excludes lands exempt from basic RPT, requires an ordinance with a public hearing (s.242), and apportions by assessed value (s.243), which in the Philippines is a fraction of market value (assessment levels fixed by ordinance, s.218).

Fit of the case to the statute: s.240 requires public works 'funded by the local government unit'. The article's PHP 39 million is described as an estimate, the right-of-way payment is 'assumed', CARES links run through private subdivision roads opened by tripartite agreements with homeowners' associations (Res. 2023-352), and sticker fees are collected by private associations; whether the city funded each link, and whether the cost base includes land, is unclear.

The PHP 476 million is an aggregate extrapolation of a per-sq-m DiD difference to the whole subdivision from sparse deed samples (the article does not give N, the number of lots, or standard errors). The article itself flags that declared deed prices may be under-reported, so deed-based DiD may understate and asking-price series may overstate.
Dates: the article says the road opened in 2013; Ordinance 02-045 (the CARES ordinance) apparently dates to 2002 (inferred from the number). 'Over 6,000 vehicles redirected' is unsourced.

Samantela & Maquiling findings are from an abstract on AGRIS and search summaries; journal, volume/year and sample size not independently confirmed; the journal is a regional UPLB periodical, so Tier 1 standing rests on university-academic authorship.
SB 1824 status unknown (filed Jan 2023; 19th Congress ended June 2025; a 20th-Congress refile was not checked).
RA 12001's effect on special-levy apportionment not checked.

No Bureau of Local Government Finance guidance, Muntinlupa budget line, tax ordinance on CARES, or ADB/World Bank study of Philippine special-levy use was found; the Milken Institute report 'Funding Transport Infrastructure Development in the Philippines: A Roadmap Toward Land Value Capture' surfaced in search but is a think-tank report (Tier 2) and was not fetched.
